draft.title: Sustainability in industry
card: Green chemistry is a way of designing chemical products and processes to reduce harm to people and the environment. It aims to prevent problems at the start, rather than clean them up afterwards.
a process is designed so fewer unwanted by-products are made. This means less waste to treat or dispose of, and less raw material lost.
hazardous reactants, solvents and products are replaced with less harmful ones where possible. This lowers risk to workers and the environment.
starting materials come from sources that are replenished, such as plants, rather than finite ones such as crude oil. Lower temperatures and pressures, or a catalyst, mean less energy is needed.
draft.remember: Green chemistry cuts harm by design: less waste, safer chemicals, renewable feedstocks and less energy.

a.q: A company changes a process so it runs at a lower temperature and pressure. Which green chemistry aim does this best meet?
a.why: Lower temperature and pressure mean less energy is needed to run the process. It does not by itself change the starting materials or how hazardous the chemicals are, so the other aims are not the main one met.
a.clue: Think about what heating and compressing use up.

b.q: Dev's company makes a plastic from crude oil. It switches to making the same plastic from sugar cane waste. Which green chemistry aim does this meet?
b.why: Sugar cane waste is a plant source that can be replaced, while crude oil is finite. The change is to the starting material. Nothing in the case says the process makes less waste or is less hazardous, so those aims cannot be assumed.
b.clue: Focus on where the starting material comes from.

check.summary: No problems found. Both questions have one clear answer that matches the card, and the card stays within the sustainability point without teaching yield, purity or the Haber process.
